items.question: "The Indian Constitution is federal in form but unitary in spirit." Critically examine the centralising features of Indian federalism.
items.modelAnswer:
The Indian Constitution establishes a **dual polity** with a distribution of powers, a written and supreme Constitution, an independent judiciary and bicameralism — the classic marks of a **federation**. Yet Article 1 deliberately calls India a **'Union of States'**, and K. C. Wheare famously described the system as **'quasi-federal'** — federal in form but unitary in spirit.

Several **centralising features** justify this description. **Legislatively**, the Union List is the largest, **residuary powers** (Art 248) rest with Parliament, and on Concurrent subjects a Union law prevails (**Art 254**); Parliament can even legislate on State List subjects (Arts 249, 250, 252, 253). **Administratively**, the Centre can issue directions to states (Arts 256-257), and the **all-India services** (Art 312) staff the higher administration of both levels. **Financially**, states depend on tax devolution and grants-in-aid recommended by the **Finance Commission** (Art 280). The Constitution also provides for a **single citizenship, single integrated judiciary, single Election Commission**, and, decisively, **emergency provisions** (Arts 352/356/360) that can turn the federal structure **unitary without any amendment**. The **Governor**, appointed by the Centre, and the frequent past misuse of **Article 356** further tilted the balance.

However, the tilt is not absolute. **S. R. Bommai (1994)** made Article 356 justiciable and affirmed **federalism as a basic feature**; the rise of **coalition politics and regional parties**, and institutions of **cooperative federalism** — the **GST Council (Art 279A)**, the **Inter-State Council**, and **NITI Aayog** — have strengthened the states' voice. For **Andhra Pradesh**, post-bifurcation dependence on central grants and the demand for special assistance illustrate how fiscal federalism plays out in practice.

In conclusion, India is best described as a **cooperative quasi-federation**: the Constitution arms the Centre for **national unity and integrity**, while evolving political and judicial practice increasingly protects state autonomy, moving the system towards genuine **cooperative and competitive federalism**.
keyPoints: Federal marks: dual polity, division of powers, written supreme Constitution, independent judiciary, bicameralism.
Article 1 'Union of States'; Wheare's 'quasi-federal' — federal in form, unitary in spirit.
Centralising features: residuary powers (248), Art 254 supremacy, Arts 249-253, all-India services, single citizenship/judiciary.
Emergency provisions (352/356/360) make the structure unitary without amendment; Centre-appointed Governor.
Counter-trends: Bommai (1994) makes federalism a basic feature; GST Council, Inter-State Council, NITI Aayog.
AP angle: post-bifurcation dependence on central grants and special-assistance demand.
items.source: Constitution of India; S. R. Bommai (1994); Sarkaria/Punchhi Reports

items.question: Discuss the recommendations of the Sarkaria and Punchhi Commissions on the use of Article 356 and the office of the Governor. How far has the S. R. Bommai judgment curbed its misuse?
items.modelAnswer:
**Article 356**, providing for President's Rule on the **failure of constitutional machinery** in a state, has been among the most contested provisions of Indian federalism. Repeated dismissal of opposition-ruled state governments led to demands for reform, addressed by successive commissions.

The **Sarkaria Commission (1983-88)** held that Article 356 should be used **very sparingly, as a last resort**, only when all alternatives fail; a warning should precede its use, and the report should be a 'speaking document'. It recommended that the **Governor** be an eminent, detached person from **outside the state**, not active in recent politics, appointed **in consultation with the Chief Minister**, and it proposed strengthening the **Inter-State Council** — a recommendation implemented in 1990. The **Punchhi Commission (2007-10)** went further: a **fixed five-year tenure** for Governors with removal only by a defined process, provision for **'localising emergencies'** to a district or part of a state rather than the whole, and clearer guidelines on the Governor's discretion in appointing Chief Ministers and reserving bills.

The decisive judicial check came in **S. R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994)**, where a nine-judge bench held that a proclamation under Article 356 is **subject to judicial review**; that the majority of a government must be tested on the **floor of the House**, not by the Governor's subjective satisfaction; that the President's power is **conditional, not absolute**; and that **secularism and federalism** are part of the basic structure. The court could **restore a dismissed government** if the proclamation was found mala fide.

Since Bommai, the **frequency of Article 356 has fallen sharply**, and floor tests have become the norm, though controversies over Governors' conduct persist. Together, the commissions' recommendations and the Bommai safeguards have substantially, if not wholly, curbed the misuse of Article 356 and pushed Indian federalism towards **greater trust and cooperation** between the Centre and the states.
keyPoints: Article 356 = President's Rule on failure of constitutional machinery; historically misused against opposition states.
Sarkaria (1983-88): Art 356 a last resort with warning; Governor a detached outsider consulted with CM; strengthen Inter-State Council.
Punchhi (2007-10): fixed 5-year Governor tenure, 'localising emergencies', clearer discretion guidelines.
S. R. Bommai (1994): Art 356 judicially reviewable; floor test decides majority; secularism/federalism basic features.
Post-Bommai: sharp fall in Art 356 use and normalisation of floor tests, though Governor controversies remain.
items.source: Sarkaria & Punchhi Commission Reports; S. R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994)

items.question: Examine the mechanisms of fiscal federalism in India. In this context, discuss the roles of the Finance Commission and the GST Council.
items.modelAnswer:
**Fiscal federalism** concerns the division of taxation powers and the transfer of resources between the Union and the states. Because the Constitution assigns the more **elastic, buoyant taxes** to the Centre while placing heavy expenditure responsibilities on the states, a structural **vertical imbalance** exists, corrected through constitutional transfer mechanisms under **Articles 268-293**.

The **Finance Commission (Art 280)** is the principal balancing wheel. Constituted by the President **every fifth year** as a quasi-judicial body of a chairman and four members, it recommends the **vertical** sharing of the divisible tax pool between the Centre and states, its **horizontal** distribution among states (using criteria such as population, area, income distance and demographic performance), and the principles of **grants-in-aid** under Article 275. The **Sixteenth Finance Commission**, chaired by **Arvind Panagariya**, will govern transfers for the award period **2026-31** *(verified 2026)*, succeeding the 15th FC under N. K. Singh. Discretionary grants under **Article 282** and, earlier, Planning Commission transfers supplemented these flows; **NITI Aayog** now serves as a policy platform rather than a fund-allocating body.

The **GST Council (Art 279A)**, created by the **101st Amendment (2016)**, marks a new institution of **cooperative fiscal federalism**. Chaired by the Union Finance Minister with state finance ministers as members, it decides tax rates, exemptions and thresholds; the **Centre holds one-third of the votes and the states two-thirds**, with every decision requiring a **three-fourths majority** — a design of **'pooled sovereignty'** in which neither level can act alone.

Challenges remain: states' loss of fiscal autonomy after subsuming their taxes into GST, delays in **compensation** payments, growing reliance on **cesses and surcharges** that shrink the divisible pool, and inter-state equity debates. For **Andhra Pradesh**, post-bifurcation revenue gaps have sharpened its stake in Finance Commission devolution. Strengthening these institutions and ensuring predictable, rule-based transfers is therefore central to a healthy **cooperative federal** fiscal order.
keyPoints: Fiscal federalism corrects vertical imbalance: Centre holds buoyant taxes, states bear high expenditure (Arts 268-293).
Finance Commission (Art 280): 5-yearly, recommends vertical & horizontal tax devolution and grants-in-aid (Art 275).
16th Finance Commission chaired by Arvind Panagariya for the award period 2026-31 (succeeds 15th FC/N. K. Singh).
GST Council (Art 279A, 101st Amendment 2016): Centre 1/3, states 2/3 votes, 3/4 majority — pooled sovereignty.
Challenges: loss of state fiscal autonomy, compensation delays, rising cesses/surcharges shrinking the divisible pool.
AP angle: post-bifurcation revenue gaps heighten dependence on Finance Commission devolution.
items.source: Constitution of India, Articles 268-293, 279A, 280; Ministry of Finance / PIB (verified Sep 2026)
